segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, careful, and occasionally contentious reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
Bleak House is a novel that begins in fog — literal fog, moral fog, the fog of a legal system that grinds lives to dust — and never quite lets you out of it.
Over the course of this series we will be unpacking its atmosphere, its characters, its architecture, and the astonishing range of its moral imagination.
Today we begin where the novel itself begins — with weather, with haunting, with the sense that something enormous and implacable is pressing down on every character in the book.
I have three quite brilliant guests with me, and I want to introduce them properly because each brings something the others cannot quite replace.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a watch — with one eye on how the mechanism works and one eye on the wonder of the thing ticking.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime resisting fashionable readings of great novels — and is almost always right to do so.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than any person alive — which means he has arguably spent more hours inside Dickens's prose than any critic breathing.
Welcome, all three of you.
Thank you — it's a genuine pleasure to be here with this novel in particular.
Bleak House is the one I return to when I want to remember what prose can actually do — what it can carry, atmospherically, before a single character has opened their mouth.
The fog in the opening is not just weather — it is Dickens constructing a moral condition in meteorological language, and doing it so well you barely notice the craft.
I am delighted to be here, though I confess I arrived with a certain wariness.
Bleak House attracts an enormous quantity of what one might charitably call thematic scaffolding — readings in which the novel becomes a manifesto rather than a story.
What I hope we shall do here is attend to the human beings inside it — whose fates are genuinely moving, and whose moral complexity is quite beyond any programme.
I'll simply say that I have read this novel aloud — all of it, every chapter — and it never once felt like work.
Which is the highest compliment I know how to pay a book.
And I want to start, if I may, with a ghost — because this novel has one of the most perfectly constructed ghost stories embedded in it that I have ever encountered.
A ghost — yes, let's begin there.
The Ghost's Walk at Chesney Wold — the curse laid upon the Dedlock family — is one of the great pieces of atmospheric storytelling in the novel.
Oliver, you've lived inside this passage — tell us what it does to you.
What it does — even now, even knowing the story — is make the hair on my arms stand up.
The setup is this: there is a crippled lady, long dead, who swore a curse on the Dedlock house.
She had walked the terrace every day despite her failing body — up and down, up and down, with greater difficulty every day.
And when her husband finally found her fallen on the pavement, she did not weep or plead.
She looked at him, Dickens says, fixedly and coldly — and spoke these words:

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
Four sentences — and they land like hammer blows.
The rhythm escalates — each sentence a little more terrible than the last — and that final imperative, let the Dedlocks listen, is chilling every single time.
What you're describing is Dickens as a rhetorician — the deliberate anaphora of those repeated 'I will walk here' clauses is almost biblical in its cadence.
Each repetition tightens the screw — and then the final clause releases the tension outward, toward all future Dedlocks.
It is a beautifully engineered piece of writing that also feels completely spontaneous — which is the hardest trick there is.
I think what moves me is the silence that precedes the curse — the years of silence between this woman and her husband.
Dickens tells us she never spoke to him on any persuasion since that night — and then, at the very end, she speaks only to damn him.
That is not atmosphere — that is character, in extremis.
And the choice to frame this as a ghost story rather than a straightforward narrative is — however reluctantly I say it — a stroke of genuine genius.
And Dickens compounds it, you see — he doesn't just give us the origin legend and leave it there.
He gives us the housekeeper, Mrs. Rouncewell, passing this story on — and the moment she does so is genuinely theatrical.
She calls the young listeners close — hither, child, towards my Lady's pillow — and then she asks them:
"Can you hear the sound upon the terrace, through the music, and the beat, and everything?"
That 'and everything' — it's so beautifully casual.
As though the ghost is competing with all of ordinary life — the music, the clock, the noise of existence — and winning.
There is something structurally brilliant about placing this legend so early in the novel — it seeds a feeling of inevitability that haunts everything that follows.
Every scene at Chesney Wold thereafter carries the ghost's footfall underneath it — whether Dickens mentions it or not.
It is the architectural equivalent of a ground bass — always present, always pressing.
That sense of fatality running beneath the surface — it's not confined to the gothic passages, is it.
Oliver, you've also been looking at the way this novel handles suffering that is more immediate — the damage done by Chancery to living people.
There's a passage where Esther hears Gridley's dying words echoed in Richard's farewell — and it struck me as one of the most quietly devastating moments in the book.
Quietly devastating is exactly right — and the quietness is everything.
The sun has gone down, the light is draining from the scene — Dickens gives us the visual darkness and then immediately tells us it is not the worst darkness in the room.
And then Esther recalls Gridley's words — a dying man's words — and they are precisely about what Chancery destroys.
"Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for.
There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!"
That final clause — the only tie Chancery has not broken — is the indictment of the whole system delivered in a single breath.
And it is the more devastating because it comes from someone already dead.
I would not quarrel with the force of that passage — but I'd note that its power is entirely human, not institutional.
What moves us is Gridley — a man of fierce spirit who has been worn to nothing — not the abstract machinery of Chancery.
Dickens is always most powerful when he grounds his indignation in a specific face, a specific grief.
That's true — and it's also worth noting how Dickens chooses to route it through Esther's narration.
She hears Gridley's words in Richard's farewell — they echo forward and backward at the same time — which is a remarkable technical achievement.
It is Esther's sensibility that makes the novel habitable — she carries grief without collapsing under it.
Before we move on, I do want to mention one more passage — because it is the comic obverse of everything we've just said, and Dickens needs both registers to be Dickens.
Harold Skimpole — that magnificent fraud — receives visitors in a room that is a perfect portrait of his soul.
Esther describes it with this wonderful accumulation of contradictions:

"It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures."
The list itself is the joke — the sheer abundance of comfort amid the squalor.
And then — there is Skimpole himself, on the sofa, in a dressing gown, drinking coffee from old china and looking at wallflowers.
At midday.
He is the novel's great comic villain — but Dickens makes you love the picture even as you despise the man.
Skimpole is a study in the aesthete who refuses all moral accountability — and Dickens anatomises him with a precision that Burke would have admired.
The shabby luxury is not merely comic detail — it is a moral condition made visible.
The man who will not pay his debts surrounds himself with every luxury — and sees no contradiction whatsoever.
And there we have the fog, the ghost, the broken, and the beautifully shameless — all within a single novel, all within a single opening hour.
In our next segment we'll be turning to the novel's two narrators — and to the extraordinary question of what Dickens gains, and risks, by splitting his story in two.
Do stay with us.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the great institutional fog of Chancery and the social spectacle of Chesney Wold.
Now we turn inward — to the individuals caught inside those systems, and what pressure does to character.
I want to begin with something that I think is easy to overlook: the children in this novel.
Dickens places children everywhere — as evidence, as accusation, as moral measure.
Edmund, you've been looking closely at two passages that place children at the centre — and they couldn't be more different in register.
They are different in register, yes — one savagely comic, the other almost unbearably sad.
And I think that tonal range is precisely the point.
Begin with Mrs. Pardiggle's unfortunate offspring.
Esther's description of these children is one of Dickens's finest comic portraits — and one of his most pointed moral arguments.
Esther observes, and I must quote this in full:
"We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that they were weazened and shrivelled — though they were certainly that too — but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent."
Ferocious with discontent.
That is not merely comic observation — it is a verdict on what organised philanthropy does to the souls nearest to it.
And the detail of young Egbert — I find it irresistible every time.
Esther says that at the mention of the Tockahoopo Indians, she could really have supposed Egbert to be one of the most baleful members of that tribe — he gave such a savage frown.
A five-year-old boy rendered as a ferocious tribesman by the sheer force of his resentment at being made to donate his pocket money.
Dickens is absolutely in his element there — grotesque caricature that is also perfectly true.
And yet there's the other child — or rather, children — and there the comedy vanishes entirely.
When Esther opens the door to that room in Chapter Fifteen, Dickens doesn't reach for comic exaggeration at all.
He reaches for something almost unbearably spare.
Here is what she finds:
"In a poor room with a sloping ceiling and containing very little furniture was a mite of a boy, some five or six years old, nursing and hushing a heavy child of eighteen months."
"There was no fire, though the weather was cold; both children were wrapped in some poor shawls and tippets as a substitute."
That phrase — as a substitute — is doing tremendous moral work in four syllables.
What ought to be warmth, parental care, security — replaced by inadequate rags.
What strikes me about that passage is the narrative restraint Dickens exercises through Esther's voice.
He doesn't editorialize — he simply opens the door and describes what is there.
The sloping ceiling, the very little furniture — these are architectural details that function as moral facts.
And the boy walking up and down, nursing and hushing — that repetition of the same verbs — it's a rhythm of exhaustion and duty.
A child performing adult care, without complaint, because there is no one else.
When I've read that passage aloud, I always feel that the prose itself has gone quiet.
There's no flourish, no Dickensian fireworks.
Just the boy, the cold, and the weight of the child on his shoulder.
That silence is its own kind of eloquence — and it is very deliberately earned against the comic noise of the Pardiggle scene.
So we have charity performed as coercion — and poverty endured as mute fact.
Let's shift to the law — and to one of the novel's great comic-menacing portraits.
Edmund, you've been looking at Vholes and the remarkable passage in which Mr. Kenge defends the indefensible.
The Vholes passages are, for my money, among the most technically accomplished satirical writing in the English novel.
The target is not merely a corrupt lawyer — it is the institutional logic that makes corruption respectable.
Listen to Kenge's defence of the system to a — as he puts it — smarting client:

"Repeal this statute, my good sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes?"
And then the magnificent conclusion:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
The horror is that Kenge is not lying — he is being perfectly logical within the assumptions of his world.
And the parliamentary committee sequence that follows is a masterclass in structural irony.
Dickens mimics the form of official inquiry — numbered questions, sworn testimony — to demonstrate how that form defeats its own purpose.
The committee establishes delay, expense, unspeakable vexation — and the answer to every question circles back to: but Mr. Vholes would be ruined.
And the fatal last answer — "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man" — is described as having proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
Respectability as a weapon of mass institutional stagnation — that's the argument in a phrase.
And then we see Vholes himself in action in Chapter Sixty — and that scene with Esther is almost more disturbing for being quieter.
He notes that he happened to record his own words in his diary — which is producible at any time, he says.
The man documents himself as he speaks.
And then, having declared Richard's affairs to be in a very bad way, his marriage ill-advised, and his prospects ruinous — he pivots to a cheerful greeting the moment Richard enters.
Dickens gives us the line verbatim:
"Am I here, sir? Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to thank you very much, sir!"
The exclamation mark on that line is doing the work of a whole indictment.
What Vholes demonstrates — and what I think is Dickens's deepest insight here — is that the most dangerous moral failures are not passionate ones.
They are procedural. Carried out. Noted in a diary that is producible at any time.
Vholes says — and this is the phrase that haunts me — "I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out."
Against that procedural cold — that willingness to destroy Richard Carstone by the book — the novel sets something quite different.
It sets warmth. Genuine feeling. And the question of what genuine feeling looks like when it is tested.
Edmund, let's turn to two characters whose goodness is very different in kind — Jarndyce on one hand, and Sir Leicester Dedlock on the other.
Jarndyce first — because the passage concerning him and the young people is extraordinarily delicate in its construction.
He is telling Richard and Ada that he had contemplated — afar off — the possibility of their union.
And the prose catches his voice with wonderful precision:

"When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
"I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
Afar off — repeated three times in the space of a breath.
It is a warning, tenderly given — but a warning nonetheless.
The parenthetical — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear — that's the moment that stops me every time.
Jarndyce breaks out of his own careful formulation to comfort Ada directly.
And the repetition — don't be shy, twice — is pure warmth uncontainable by syntax.
Dickens understood that the deepest characterisation happens in exactly these small grammatical ruptures.
It's a beautiful speech to read aloud because of precisely that — the sentence keeps trying to be formal and the feeling keeps breaking through.
Jarndyce is a man whose goodness is constitutionally unable to hold its shape under the pressure of actual affection.
And that, against the chilling precision of Vholes, is the moral architecture Dickens is constructing.
And then there is Sir Leicester — who is, I would argue, the novel's most surprising moral achievement.
He has been comic, pompous, magnificently absurd.
And then he is tested — by the revelation of his wife's secret — and rises to it in a way that silences the comedy entirely.
The narrator's assessment is precise and earned:
"His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true."
And then the extraordinary final sentence:
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Children of the dust — aristocrat and mechanic alike.
That is not a social programme — that is a moral vision.
What's remarkable structurally is how Dickens has prepared us for that moment.
We have seen Sir Leicester's absurdity at such length that when his dignity arrives, it carries absolute authority.
The narrator says his formal array of words might at any other time have something ludicrous in it.
That acknowledgement of his ludicrousness is what makes the reversal devastating rather than sentimental.
Children of the dust shine equally — what a place to rest for a moment.
We've moved from the savage frowns of the Pardiggle children to the cold room where a five-year-old nurses his sister — and from Vholes's monstrous procedure to Sir Leicester's unexpected grace.
The novel is making an argument about moral possibility — even inside systems designed to crush it.
In our next segment, we'll be asking what the two narrative voices — Esther's and the omniscient narrator's — are doing to each other throughout the novel.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we read Dickens's great novel slowly, carefully, and with the attention it deserves.
Today's segment is called The Architecture of Secrets — and secrets, in Bleak House, are not merely plot devices.
They are the load-bearing walls of the entire novel.
With me today are three guests who bring very different but equally sharp eyes to the text.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with enormous pleasure in how the parts fit together.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the moral imagination is where great fiction lives — and has little patience for readings that flatten character into symbol.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Let's begin with the man who arrives at Chesney Wold at sunset — Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Tulkinghorn is one of the great entrances in all of Dickens.
He doesn't storm in, he doesn't hurry — he simply appears, at his usual methodical pace.
And Dickens gives us this extraordinary sentence about what he carries.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb, every crease — the man is literally made of other people's concealed lives.
When I've read this aloud, I always slow down on "crease" — it's physical, almost tactile, and slightly sinister.
Dickens is writing for the voice here, no question.
What strikes me is the parenthetical Dickens slips in — "if it be a mask" — referring to Tulkinghorn's expressionless face.
That tiny hesitation is doing enormous structural work.
The narrator cannot quite say whether Tulkinghorn has a self beneath the surface — or whether the surface is all there is.
And then Dickens extends it with a beautiful symmetry — he keeps the secrets of his clients, and he is his own client.
"He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
The sentence folds back on itself, exactly as Tulkinghorn does.
Form and content are perfectly fused — that's Dickens at his most controlled.
I think we mustn't let the style seduce us away from what the passage is actually doing morally.
Tulkinghorn is not merely a stylistic effect — he is a study in a particular kind of corruption.
The question Dickens poses — whether his soul is devoted to the great or whether he sells them nothing beyond his services — is a question about whether such a man has any inner life at all.
Dr. Johnson would have recognised the type immediately — the man who has so thoroughly subordinated himself to utility that the self has quietly evaporated.
That is a moral horror, not merely a narrative device.
And this moral horror, as Sir Edmund puts it, is precisely what makes the scene on the terrace so quietly unbearable.
Because Tulkinghorn arrives bearing information — a message, delivered through Sir Leicester, that tips Lady Dedlock's world on its axis.
Oliver, you've described this scene as a masterclass in comic misdirection that conceals genuine dread — tell us more.
It is comic, or at least it begins that way — Sir Leicester fumbling with the letter, losing his place, searching for his eye-glass.
"He says — I beg your pardon, that's not the place. He says — yes! Here I have it!"
That's pure performance — the dashes, the false starts, the little triumph of "yes!" — Dickens has notated it like a script.
And meanwhile Lady Dedlock sits there looking, the narrator tells us, a little irritated.
But when the message finally arrives — and here is the real sting — it is Tulkinghorn's voice in the room even in his absence.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words at the end. "I have seen him." The comedy evaporates on the spot.
The structural audacity of delivering that information through Sir Leicester is what I find breathtaking.
He is utterly oblivious — looking at the fire, confident of his wife's perfect respectability, renewing what the narrator calls his "stately protest."
He is the conduit for a message that is, in effect, a threat — and he carries it without the slightest awareness of its weight.
Dickens is using dramatic irony as architecture — it holds the scene up.
Sir Leicester is easy to patronise, and readers often do.
But I think Dickens's portrait of him is more generous than it first appears.
His trust in Lady Dedlock is absolute and unexamined — which is, in the context of a novel about hidden knowledge, a kind of innocence.
He has the expression, the narrator says, of the Dedlock on the staircase — ancestral impassivity — while his wife and his lawyer engage in a silent duel above his head.
There is genuine pathos in that image, not merely satire.
And that silent duel brings us to perhaps the most extraordinary passage in this chapter — the narrator's meditation on what Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn each conceal from the other.
Eleanor, this passage about their mutual watching — you've called it one of the great sentences in Victorian fiction.
I'll stand by that claim.
Dickens builds it as a series of parallel clauses, each one tightening the screw.

"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows —"
"— all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
Three "whether" clauses — each one a question the narrator refuses to answer — and then that door closes shut: "hidden, for the time."
"For the time" is doing quiet, devastating work — it promises that this concealment will not hold forever.
The entire novel's plot is encoded in those three words.
Reading that passage aloud is a genuine challenge — because the structure demands a kind of relentless forward pressure, and then the full stop arrives and you have to let it land.
The phrase "customary deportment" is wonderfully dry — both of them performing normalcy while the ground shifts beneath them.
It's theatrical in the deepest sense — two actors who know exactly what the other is doing and neither will break character.
The mutual watching Dickens describes — that is what great antagonists do on stage.
What strikes me is that Dickens grants Tulkinghorn no inner life here, but he refuses to say so directly.
The passage is scrupulously agnostic — "whether... whether... what" — and that epistemological modesty is itself the point.
We cannot know what such people think because such people have made themselves unknowable — which is a moral condition, not merely a narrative convenience.
Burke understood this: the person who entirely conceals themselves from others eventually conceals themselves from themselves.
From the sealed world of Chesney Wold, I want to move to a very different kind of secret — the secrets of Chancery, and the human wreckage it leaves behind.
Eleanor, you've been looking at the figure of Gridley — the man from Shropshire — and what he reveals about the novel's deeper argument.
Gridley is fascinating because he arrives in the novel as pure energy — rage, almost ungovernable, and yet there's a terrible dignity in him.
He apologises to Esther for his lack of polish, and then explains it in one of the most scalding lines in the book.
"I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of treading upon velvet."
"Burning iron" and "velvet" — those two textures in the same sentence compress twenty-five years of suffering into something you feel in your body.
And the identity question he raises — "I am the man from Shropshire" — is heartbreaking precisely because he's been reduced to a joke.
Chancery's cruelty is in making him famous for being its victim — his suffering is their entertainment.
He beats one hand on the other, the narrator tells us — passionately.
That physical detail is everything — he has no other resource left but his own body as witness to his outrage.
Compare that with Tulkinghorn — who carries secrets in every crease of his dress, perfectly still, perfectly composed.
Dickens has arranged these two figures as a kind of visual argument: the system and its human cost, side by side.
Gridley is not merely a victim, though — and I think that matters enormously.
He beg's Esther's pardon for his lack of politeness — twice, in the space of a breath.
The instinct toward courtesy survives even twenty-five years of grinding humiliation — and that is a statement about character, about individual moral resilience.
Dickens is too honest a novelist to make Gridley simply a placard for institutional injustice.
That question of individual character — its resilience and its concealment — brings us to the final passage for today.
It's a passage from Esther's narration, in which Mr. Jarndyce reveals to her what little he knows of the woman who kept herself hidden — the woman who, he says, is Esther's aunt.
Edmund, this is where the novel's secret architecture becomes almost geometrically beautiful — your thoughts?
What Jarndyce reveals here is a story told entirely in negatives — what the mysterious lady would not say, would not do, would never disclose.
Dickens frames it with a careful legal precision — Mr. Kenge is the accredited agent, the disclosure is shaped like a deposition.
And at the centre of this legal construction sits the phrase Jarndyce reports with such scrupulous fidelity.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
"The steadfastness of her resolution" — Dickens honours the will it takes to maintain such secrecy, even as we suspect it is destroying her.
This is not mere concealment — it is a form of suffering chosen and maintained.
And Dickens has placed this revelation in Esther's narrative — which matters enormously to how we receive it.
Esther is hearing, in the third person, the story of her own origins — mediated through Jarndyce, who heard it from Kenge, who heard it from a woman who gave a false name.
It's a chain of transmission in which every link is a concealment.
And Jarndyce closes it with the most unbearable simplicity: "My dear, I have told you all."
"My dear, I have told you all."
He has told her everything — and almost nothing.
"My dear, I have told you all" — four words that would break any actor's heart to deliver correctly.
Because Jarndyce means it with such complete tenderness — he has given her everything he has — and yet what he has is almost nothing.
The name assumed, the aunt who will never speak, the resolution that will never bend — and somewhere behind all of it, a connection the novel is slowly, inexorably drawing tighter.
Dickens knows exactly how long to let the reader sit in that incompleteness before he pulls the next thread.

Tulkinghorn's sealed face, Sir Leicester's oblivious letter-reading, Gridley beating his own hand in rage, and Esther receiving an inheritance of withheld information — these are the pillars of the architecture Dickens has built.
Secrets in Bleak House are not simply hidden — they are structural, load-bearing, and eventually lethal.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan — three guides who make the darkness of this novel genuinely illuminating.
We'll continue in our next segment — deeper into the fog.

segments.title: The Comic Life of Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart, passage by passage, to find out what makes it tick.

I'm your host, and today we're looking at the young lovers at the heart of the book — Richard Carstone and Ada Clare — and what the novel says, sometimes tenderly, sometimes with a quiet chill, about love and vocation.
With me today are three wonderful guides to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who reads Dickens for the craft — the architecture underneath the story.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the greatness of fiction lies in its moral imagination, in the testing of individual character.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, narrator of more classic novels than anyone alive — brings the performer's ear to every passage we discuss.
Let's begin with Esther's account of Richard and Ada confiding in her — a scene that is sweet and serious at the same time.
What I love about this scene — and I've read it aloud more times than I can count — is the way Esther positions herself.
Richard and Ada flank her on either side and, as Esther puts it, seemed to have fallen in love with me instead of one another.
That little parenthesis Dickens drops in is the key to Esther's whole narrative voice — she's self-deprecating but she knows exactly what she's doing.
And then there's this marvellous confession she makes about letting them run on.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That semicolon does all the work — the little dash of guilty pleasure before she pulls herself back into the role of sensible guardian.
Oliver's right about the voice, and I want to push that a little further, because what Dickens is doing structurally here is quite audacious.
Esther is the narrator, she's supposed to be the reliable centre, and yet she openly admits she was caught up in the romance.
That moment of self-indulgence destabilises the reader's trust — just slightly, just enough to make you wonder what else she might be editing.
But what I find even more impressive is the sentence that follows — when Esther turns the scene towards duty.

"How it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Three abstract nouns — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — dropped in a row, and somehow they don't feel like a sermon.
They feel like a foreboding.
Eleanor's word — foreboding — is precisely right, and it is worth dwelling on why.
Dickens is not being cynical about young love here.
He is identifying with great precision the specific weakness of character that will undo Richard Carstone.
Richard can say he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada.
The saying of it comes easily to a young man of natural warmth and good feeling.
The doing of it is another matter entirely — and that, I would argue, is the whole moral engine of his story.
And Jarndyce sees it too, doesn't he — long before Richard himself does.
Let's turn to his address to the young couple, which is one of the most carefully written scenes in these early chapters.
Jarndyce's speech to Ada and Richard is, for my money, one of Dickens's finest pieces of sustained moral rhetoric.
He does not condescend, he does not threaten, he does not hedge with sentimentality.
He offers them a remarkable gift — the gift of being known in their possible future failure without judgment.
The passage is worth quoting in full, but this is the heart of it.

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Nothing monstrous or uncommon.
The double negative carries enormous tenderness — and enormous knowledge of the world.
What I notice performing that speech — and I've done it — is the parenthesis that Dickens tucks in: your manhood will excuse me, Rick.
It's the kindest little safety valve in the novel.
Jarndyce is essentially saying to a young man: you might fall out of love, and that's all right.
And he knows that merely saying it risks wounding Richard's pride.
So he wraps it in a little bow of mock-formal deference — your manhood will excuse me — and the whole thing is disarmed.
Dickens had the social intelligence of a diplomat and the timing of a comedian.
I want to add one thing about the structure of Jarndyce's two speeches taken together, because I think they're a diptych.
The first speech — the one Edmund quoted — is about love and the softness of the heart.
The second speech turns entirely to will and effort.
And the pivot is one of the most elegant sentences in the chapter.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that one image does the work of a whole sermon.
Jarndyce's point is precise: Richard is already inclined to sit back and let fate do its work — in love, in Chancery, in everything.
And Jarndyce makes the stakes absolutely plain at the end of that speech.
He says — and the severity of it is bracing — that if Richard expects Fortune to do the work, he must leave Ada here.

"If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
Leave your cousin Ada here.
The entire novel is in that ultimatum — and Richard, of course, will not heed it.
Before we move on, I want to bring in a quite different voice on Richard — Mrs. Badger's clinical assessment of his aptitude for medicine.
Oliver, this is your territory — the comic grotesque becoming something more uncomfortable.
Mrs. Badger is one of those Dickens creations you treasure for the comedy and then feel slightly ashamed of, because she turns out to be exactly right.
Her manner is all drawing-room delicacy — My dear Miss Summerson — but the diagnosis underneath is devastating.
She says Richard feels languid about the profession — languid, mind you, not incompetent, not untalented.
And then she holds up Allan Woodcourt as the contrast.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
She's describing a vocation — the willingness to suffer cheerfully for the thing you love.
And that, of course, is precisely what Richard cannot do.
What's so clever about that passage structurally is that Mrs. Badger introduces Woodcourt almost accidentally — as a counterexample.
But Dickens is doing something far more deliberate: he's seeding the novel with its eventual moral hero at the precise moment his foil is being found wanting.
Richard drifts; Woodcourt endures.
The contrast is planted here, quietly, and it will echo for hundreds of pages.
And the novel ends this sequence of passages with an image that I think none of us can quite shake off.
Esther watches Ada and Richard walk through a sunlit room and out into shadow — and Edmund, I'd love your reading of that moment.
It is, I think, the most beautiful and the most quietly terrible passage in the early part of the novel.
Esther watches them pass down the adjoining room, Richard talking earnestly, Ada looking up at him — utterly absorbed in one another.
And then Dickens writes this.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Esther does not comment.
Dickens allows the weather to speak, and it speaks with terrible clarity.
When I read that passage aloud I always find myself slowing involuntarily on the word lightly.
They went on lightly — and there is something in that word that knows too much.
The lightness of people who do not yet know what is coming.
I've read a great many novels, and very few writers — very few — can make a change in the weather feel like a death sentence delivered in advance.
The thing that strikes me technically is the shift in Esther's focalization at that moment.
For most of the scene Esther reports what she sees — he talked, she listened.
But in those final sentences she moves into something almost omniscient — she is not just watching them, she is somehow watching time.
Their happy thoughts traversing the years to come — she can see their imagined future from the outside, and she knows it is wrong.
It is a moment of narrative sleight of hand so accomplished you barely notice it — and it breaks your heart.
So young, so full of promise — and the sun already clouding over.
That image captures something essential about what Bleak House does — the simultaneous tenderness and dread with which it regards human hope.
We'll be back after the break to look at what happens when that hope begins to curdle — and Richard begins to lose his way.

segments.title: A Child's Witness: Jo and the Cost of Indifference

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're deep inside Chapter Eleven today, and the novel has taken us somewhere genuinely disturbing.
A coroner's inquest. A nameless dead man. And a crossing-sweeper boy called Jo.
With me today are three voices I'm very glad to have in the room.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley — novelist, teacher, and close reader of how great fiction is actually built.
Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don, moral reader of fiction, and a man who believes character is everything.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator, and someone who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone alive.
Let's start with Jo's testimony at the inquest — that extraordinary moment when the novel introduces us to this boy properly.
What strikes me first about the Jo passage is how Dickens strips the prose down to match the character.
The sentences are short. The vocabulary is elemental. It's almost percussive.
And then Dickens gives us this extraordinary list of negatives.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Each denial lands like a door being shut in turn.
And then the extraordinary question: "What's home?"
Not — he has no home. But — the concept itself is unavailable to him.
That is craft of the highest order.
And if you read that passage aloud — which I have done, many times — the rhythm does the work for you.
"Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on." Those full stops are rests in a score.
Dickens is writing for a voice, not just an eye.
But what moves me every time — every single time — is the moral logic at the end of that passage.
This boy who knows nothing knows two things: a broom is a broom, and it's wicked to tell a lie.
"Don't recollect who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both."
Society has given him nothing — and yet moral instinct survived anyway. That's quietly devastating.
I think Oliver puts his finger on the essential thing, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What we are witnessing in Jo is not a social programme — it is a study in natural goodness.
He knows nothing of institutions, of church, of school. And yet he will tell the truth.
Dickens is making a very old argument — older than any Reform Act — about the seat of conscience.
The novel earns its indignation because it first establishes the humanity of its object.
Jo is not a statistic. He is a soul. And Dickens never lets us forget it.
And that humanity is tested further when Jo takes the stand and speaks about the dead man — the mysterious Nemo.
Eleanor, you've been looking closely at what Jo actually tells the inquest about their relationship.
Yes — and this is where the chapter becomes almost unbearably tender.
We're told that Jo recognised the dead man by his yellow face and black hair.
And then we get the memory of a single cold winter night. A doorway. A shivering boy.
The man turns back. Questions him. And having found that he had not a friend in the world, says —
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
The exclamation mark after 'Not one' is doing so much. It's recognition, solidarity, maybe even relief.
Two people utterly abandoned by the world find each other in a doorway. That's the whole novel in miniature.
I've read that line in recording booths, and I have never once got through it without something catching.
Because the simplicity of it is devastating. "Neither have I. Not one."
There's no rhetoric. No Dickensian flourish. Just two men in the dark, equally lost.
And then we learn that Nemo used to ask Jo strange questions — whether he slept sound at night, how he bore cold and hunger, whether he ever wished to die.
Questions a father might ask. Or a man contemplating his own exit from the world.
The ambiguity there is extraordinarily dark. And Dickens plants it and walks on.
One mustn't overlook what that portrait of Nemo tells us about character as well.
Here is a man who has failed utterly — professionally, socially, by every measurable standard.
And yet his one recorded act of agency in this novel is an act of pure generosity toward a child in a doorway.
Dickens is making a claim about the irreducibility of the moral self — that it survives even the most comprehensive ruin.
That is not a political argument. That is a theological one. And Dickens earns it fully.
Before we leave the inquest entirely, there's one voice we haven't yet given its due — Mrs. Piper.
Oliver, I suspect you have a view on Mrs. Piper.
A view! I have a profound and undying love for Mrs. Piper.
She is one of those Dickensian supporting characters who arrives, detonates, and leaves the furniture rearranged.
The description of her testimony is a masterclass in comic prose rhythm.
Dickens sets it up perfectly: she has a good deal to say, but not much to tell.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
'Chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation' — that is Dickens describing half of human conversation in nine words.
And then the comedy deepens. She refers to the deceased throughout as 'the plaintive.'
"The plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself."
The whole apparatus of the law, rendered absurd by one woman's magnificent confusion about vocabulary.
And yet the comedy is load-bearing. It isn't decorative.
Mrs. Piper's rambling parentheses actually reveal the texture of the neighbourhood gossip that surrounded Nemo in life.
He was feared, rumoured about, considered dangerous to children. That is the community's verdict on him — built from nothing but air and 'his feariocious air.'
And then Jo's testimony cuts clean through all of that.
The boy who was actually spoken to — the one exception in Nemo's total isolation — tells a completely different story.
Dickens is doing something forensic with point of view here. Who sees? Who knows? Who gets to say?
The contrast between the inquest as institution and Jo as witness is rather the heart of the chapter, I think.
The law cannot hear Jo. He is dismissed — ruled incompetent to give evidence — because he cannot identify the Bible.
And so the one person who actually knew the dead man is silenced by the very process designed to establish the truth about him.
That is not merely a social critique — it is a tragedy of epistemology. We cannot know, because we have arranged things so that we cannot know.
And the chapter doesn't end with the inquest. It ends with something far quieter, and perhaps more haunting.
Eleanor, you've been sitting with those final images — the vigil over Nemo's body, and Jo at the gate.
Yes. And I want to put these two images together, because I think they're in deliberate conversation.
First: the body watched through the night by — and this is the detail that undoes me — 'the gaunt eyes in the shutters.'
It's as if the building itself is keeping watch, because no human being will.
And then Dickens imagines this man as a child at his mother's breast, nestled, beloved. The prose becomes almost unbearably delicate.
"A little child, with eyes upraised to her loving face, and soft hand scarcely knowing how to close upon the neck to which it crept."
And then the cry that follows: "where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
Every human being was once that child. Dickens insists we feel it.
The indifference of the world to this death is made monstrous by that image of the child.
And then the second image you mentioned — Jo at the gate. That is the chapter's final gesture, and it is almost silent.
The narrator calls Jo 'it' throughout this passage. Not 'he.' 'It.'
Which on one level is devastating — the world's refusal to grant him full personhood.
And yet what 'it' does is this.
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
'Softly.' That single adverb breaks the heart.
No speech. No tears. Just this boy, with his broom, paying the only tribute he knows how to give.
It is a profound image of faithfulness. And it asks very little of us to receive it.
Jo cannot write. He cannot pray — or not in any form the church would recognise. He cannot even speak well.
But he can sweep. And so he sweeps.
Dickens understands, as the greatest moralists have always understood, that love expresses itself through action — however small, however inadequate, however unseen.
The archway, made clean. As fine a sentence of farewell as anything in this novel.
Jo sweeping the step — and the mother who will never know where her son lies.
Chapter Eleven leaves us with these images — and they don't fade quickly.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan — this has been a conversation worth having.
We'll continue our journey through Bleak House in the next episode.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we read Dickens's great novel slowly, carefully, and with proper relish.
I'm joined today by three voices I'm very glad to have at this table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great gift is making the architecture of fiction feel as exciting as the story itself.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral investigations — stories of character tested by circumstance, of goodness and sacrifice and the limits of will.

And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Dickens first as a performer, alive to the rhythms and the comic timing and the moments that were written for the voice.
Today's segment is called Narration as Moral Act — and we want to ask what Dickens does when he steps back, or forward, or sideways, to pass judgment on what he's showing us.

Edmund, let me come to you first — because the passages before us range from Jarndyce's great tirade against Chancery to an extraordinary direct address to a child named Jo, and I think that range matters enormously.
It does matter, and I think it matters in a way that resists the politicised reading one so often encounters with this novel.

What strikes me first about Jarndyce's account of the suit is not the satire of institutions — though that is vivid enough — but the moral portrait of a man who has learned, at enormous personal cost, not to think.
Dickens gives us the machinery of Chancery through a voice that is itself on the verge of breaking.
Listen to what Jarndyce actually says — and the rhythm of it is everything.
"And thus, through years and years, and lives and lives, everything goes on, constantly beginning over and over again, and nothing ever ends."
That repetition — years and years, lives and lives — is not rhetorical decoration.
It enacts the very circularity it describes — you feel the grinding of the wheel even as you read the sentence.
And that sentence builds to a full stop that feels like a door slamming in an empty house.
I've read that passage aloud many times and I never quite find the right speed for it — because Dickens is doing two things simultaneously.
He's giving you the comedy — the infernal country-dance of costs and fees, the history of the apple pie — that is pure Dickensian music hall.
And then, without warning, the trap door opens and you're in genuine tragedy.
He even warns you with that last line — 'But it won't do to think of it!' — which is itself a kind of desperate humor over an abyss.
What I find structurally extraordinary is that Dickens gives this speech to a character who is himself trapped — Jarndyce can't exit the suit, as he says, on any terms.
So the narration of the indictment is folded inside the very condition it indicts — Jarndyce is a man lecturing on a prison from inside the prison cell.
That's not satire of institutions in the abstract — that's character-embodied moral argument, which is a much harder thing to achieve.
Precisely — and that distinction matters to me a great deal.
Dickens is at his greatest not when he is a pamphleteer but when the indignation is inseparable from the human being who carries it.
Which brings me to the passage about Jo — which is, if anything, the more radical technical choice.
The omniscient narrator, in a single short passage, addresses a child directly — 'Jo, is it thou?' — and in doing so shifts the entire moral register of the novel.
The courts have dismissed Jo — he cannot give evidence, he is a rejected witness — and the narrator steps in, as it were, to hold the court of last appeal.
And the evidence the narrator accepts is this — let me read it as Dickens wrote it.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That child's broken English is not corrected, not condescended to — it is received as testimony.
I have to tell you, when I first recorded that passage, I had to stop after those words.
Not for theatrical effect — I just found I couldn't go on for a moment.
'He wos wery good to me, he wos' — that doubling of the final 'he wos' is where Dickens earns everything.
It's the rhythm of a child reassuring himself of something he can barely hold onto.
The misspelling — 'wery' — is usually read as comedy in Dickens, as it is with Sam Weller elsewhere.
Here it is pure grief — and Dickens knows that, and he trusts the reader to feel the shift.
That shift in register is something I want to linger on — because it's achieved through a switch in narrative mode, not just in tone.
For most of the novel, Esther narrates in the first person — intimate, self-deprecating, occasionally unreliable.
The omniscient narrator runs in parallel, and that narrator is the one who can address Jo directly — who has the standing, as it were, to speak for the dispensation that the courts deny.
It's a structural choice with a moral function — the two-narrator architecture is not a technical experiment, it is itself an argument about where truth lives.
I should like to turn, if we may, to another passage that I think shows Dickens operating at a different register altogether — the account of Lady Dedlock's sister.
This is Jarndyce speaking to Esther — and he is describing a sacrifice that nobody but the woman herself ever fully understood.
The passage is worth reading in full, because the syntax carries everything.

"She wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
And then: "In consideration for those master points in him, and even in consideration for them in herself, she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it."
'Live in it and die in it' — that parallelism does something no amount of editorial commentary could.
It seals her fate in the very sentence that describes her choice.
The phrase 'which were both her nature too' is doing something almost invisible — and it's where Dickens's moral sympathy is at its most precise.
She doesn't sacrifice herself despite her pride — she sacrifices herself because of her pride, because she recognizes his pride, because they are the same.
Dickens renders that not through authorial explanation but through the compression of a single subordinate clause.
And 'Certainly he never saw her, never heard of her from that hour. Nor did any one.'
Three words — 'Nor did any one' — and the woman simply ceases to exist.
That is Dickens at his most ruthless — the novel takes her at her word, and simply closes the door.
The final passage I want to raise is Inspector Bucket's appeal to Jarndyce — which is a rather different kind of moral narration.
It is spoken by a character who is, by profession, a detective — a man whose intelligence is entirely in service of reading other people.
And yet what he says is genuinely moral — not merely strategic.
He tells Jarndyce — and the phrasing is exact — let me read it.

"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly."
'I ask no question, and I say no more than that' — in those words Bucket performs the same restraint he is asking Jarndyce to exercise.
He knows the secret, he will not name it, and he makes his appeal entirely on the grounds of what a humane heart must do.
Bucket is one of the great performances in the novel — and I use that word deliberately.
He is always reading his audience — 'Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest attention all along' — and adjusting his delivery accordingly.
In that way he is not entirely unlike a novelist.
Or an actor, for that matter.
And that likeness is not accidental — because the urgency Bucket generates in that speech is achieved through the same tools Dickens uses throughout the novel.
Time is weaponised — 'eight or ten hours worth a hundred pound apiece,' then a thousand — the rhetoric escalates to force a decision.
It is a moral argument made through the grammar of emergency — and it works on the reader exactly as it works on Jarndyce.
What emerges from all of these passages, it seems to me, is that Dickens never simply tells us what to feel — he constructs the conditions under which we cannot feel otherwise.

Whether it's the grinding repetition of the Chancery machinery, the broken grammar of a child, the parallelism of a woman's self-imposed death, or the escalating clock of a detective's appeal — each time, the form is the argument.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — thank you.
We'll continue our exploration of Bleak House in the next segment.
We come now to our closing segment — and it feels right to end where Bleak House itself so often ends: with characters in the grip of forces larger than themselves.
We've been circling all episode around the question of survival — who endures in this novel, and at what cost.
Eleanor, you've been sitting with four passages that together span something extraordinary — from high satire to pure tragedy.
I'd like you to take us in. Where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with Lady Dedlock, because I think she's the novel's great illustration of a certain terrible irony.
She believes herself utterly unknowable — an inscrutable being, as Dickens puts it, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
And yet every tradesperson, every maid, every deferential hanger-on has mapped her with surgical precision.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary image of how they operate — let me read it, because the simile is one of the novel's comic masterstrokes.

They are people who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience, lead her and her whole troop after them — who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput.
Lilliput. Of all things.
The aristocracy as a helpless miniature fleet, towed away by their own jewellers and librarians.
And what makes that simile so perfect is the scale of it — Gulliver, of all giants, being the one conscripted to make the aristocracy feel small.
But I also love the Mr. Sladdery passage — the librarian, of all people, who repeats his phrase with such magnificent self-satisfaction.
He says — and I do need to read this aloud, because the rhythm is everything —

"If you want to get this print upon the tables of my high connexion, sir — you must leave it, if you please, to me, for I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion, sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my finger."
And then Dickens adds, perfectly deadpan: in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all.
That parenthetical is the whole joke and the whole horror at once.
It is very funny. And one should not apologise for saying so — Dickens earns the laughter before he earns the dread.
But what strikes me about these passages together is the progression Dickens constructs from the comic to the absolutely stark.
We move from Lady Dedlock being managed by her jewellers to Tulkinghorn standing in a doorway above a dying man.
The passage describing Nemo is one of the most physically precise pieces of prose in the entire novel.
There is no sentiment — only sensation. What Tulkinghorn sees, smells, and then, most disturbingly, tastes.
That detail of taste is what I find most devastating about the passage.
Dickens moves through the senses in order — sight, smell — and then arrives somewhere utterly unexpected.
The sentence builds toward it so carefully — listen to how it arrives:
through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.
The lawyer's mouth. Not the room. Not Nemo's. The contamination has already crossed.
That is Dickens showing us how far poverty can reach — even into the body of the man who has come to investigate it.
And there is something about the candle in that passage that I can't let go of.
The wick has burned so long it has doubled over — and Dickens calls what it leaves above it a tower of winding-sheet.
A shroud, built by the candle itself, hovering over the dying man. He hasn't been attended to. Even his light has given up tidily before him.
When I read passages like that aloud, I have to slow down simply to let the image form in the air.
And then there is Mrs. Snagsby. Which is an altogether different register — but no less relentless.
Eleanor, your third passage — she becomes his shadow. Permanently. The prose makes it feel like a curse being formally laid.
There is something almost liturgical about the language Dickens uses at the close of that chapter.
Exactly — and I think that passage is one of the most audacious comic-gothic fusions in the book.
It begins with this marvellous image: a ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped, following him through the house.
And then the prose rises into something almost incantatory — hear the repetition:
And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own.

And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow.
Bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh — that is marriage vow language. Dickens has inverted the covenant completely.
What was meant to sanctify union now describes a domestic surveillance state of one.
Shadow of his shadow. That final phrase. It lands like a door closing.
I've read a great many comic Gothic passages aloud over the years, and very few achieve that — the moment where the comic and the genuinely eerie become indistinguishable.
Poor Mr. Snagsby. He never had much of a spine, and now he hasn't even a shadow to call his own.
But Dickens does not let us end there — in satire or in horror. He gives us Ada.
The fourth passage — Richard failing, and Ada kneeling beside him — is, I think, the most purely moving thing in Eleanor's selection today.
I distrust easy sentiment in fiction. But this is not easy. It has been earned across hundreds of pages.
And it is rendered with almost liturgical simplicity through Esther's eyes.
What Dickens does in that passage structurally is fascinating — the scene is almost entirely gesture and image. No dialogue. No interiority.
Esther simply describes what she sees. And that restraint is what breaks you open.
The passage reads:
my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me.
And then Esther adds, simply: Oh, what a loving and devoted face I saw.
The exclamation is not theatrical — it is overwhelmed. Esther cannot describe the face; she can only attest to it.
The golden hair falling like sunlight on his head. It's a halo. Dickens gives Richard a halo — borrowed from Ada's devotion.
He has wasted everything — his fortune, his health, his future — and she kneels in the posture of a pietà.
I find that passage almost impossible to read aloud without a pause before the final line. The silence earns the moment.
And I think that image — the silence earning the moment — might be the best summary of what Bleak House does across its entire length.
It accumulates — the satire, the horror, the domestic grotesque — and then Ada kneels down, and all of it converges.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you all. This has been exactly the conversation the novel deserves.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then, keep reading — and keep listening for what the silence is doing.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c7:p69.text:
“Now, come hither,” says the housekeeper. “Hither, child, towards my
Lady’s pillow. I am not sure that it is dark enough yet, but listen!
Can you hear the sound upon the terrace, through the music, and the
beat, and everything?”
c7:p69.summary: Mrs. Rouncewell asks the young listeners to detect the Ghost's Walk footsteps on the terrace despite the loud clock music and machinery noise.
c7:p69.best_quote: Can you hear the sound upon the terrace, through the music, and the beat, and everything?

c24:p154.text:
The sun was down, the light had gradually stolen from the roof, and
the shadow had crept upward. But to me the shadow of that pair, one
living and one dead, fell heavier on Richard’s departure than the
darkness of the darkest night. And through Richard’s farewell words I
heard it echoed: “Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits
and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul
alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many
suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on
earth that Chancery has not broken!”
c24:p154.summary: Esther reflects on Gridley's final words, which echo through her memory and Richard's departure, reinforcing the novel's commentary on Chancery's destructive power.
c24:p154.best_quote: Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!

c43:p23.text:
We went upstairs to the first floor, still seeing no other furniture
than the dirty footprints. Mr. Jarndyce without further ceremony

my great uncle, poor Tom Jarndyce, began to think of it, it was the

injury which her haughty spirit had received in her cause of quarrel
with her sister had wounded her beyond all reason, but she wrote him

truth she did—and that the resolution was exacted from her by her
knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which
were both her nature too. In consideration for those master points in
him, and even in consideration for them in herself, she made the

both, I fear; certainly he never saw her, never heard of her from

c56:p51.text:
“Now, Mr. Jarndyce”—Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest
attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one
o’clock. When one strikes, there’s another hour gone, and it’s worth
a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput

c10:p66.text:
For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and
trousers, with bare feet. He has a yellow look in the spectral
darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of
its wick (still burning) has doubled over and left a tower of
winding-sheet above it. His hair is ragged, mingling with his
whiskers and his beard—the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the
scum and mist around him, in neglect. Foul and filthy as the room is,
foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes
those are which most oppress the senses in it; but through the
general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco,
there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.
c10:p66.summary: Tulkinghorn discovers a man on a low, filthy bed—Nemo—dressed in shirt and trousers, spectral and yellowed, with long unkempt hair and whiskers, and the sickly air redolent of stale tobacco and opium.

c25:p58.text:
A ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped, follows the law-stationer
to the room he came from and glides higher up. And henceforth he
begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his
own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his
own. And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may
pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs.
Snagsby is there too—bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of
his shadow.
c25:p58.summary: The chapter ends with Mrs. Snagsby becoming a permanent ghostly shadow following Snagsby, inseparable from him and present in all his secretive dealings.
